doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: Live TV nerves on SNL and Letterman, and spontaneity
summary: He describes SNL's live production, Letterman's mistakes left in, Paul Simon's cut-off song and Al Chez's remark about faking it.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Was being live on SNL or Late Night, was it nerve wracking?
Or did you get used to it?

Well it was really exciting on SNL, how live it was. At the beginning totally nerve wracking. I couldn’t believe it was going to happen during the rehearsals leading up to it. How complicated the production of the show was — I never had seen anything like it. The studio that seemed huge at the time, and they had so many different sets as they still do. You can see it on SNL now when the camera pulls back you see the studio with all

the different sets that they’re going to use during the half hour, all at different points, and how are they going to go from here to here? Well the whole camera’s like a big caravan drive down during the commercial to the other end. I said this is surreal but it certainly happened. And every time was pretty exciting because you know you don’t get a second chance, period. You don’t get a do-over. Nonetheless Letterman was really more spontaneous because yes you could do something over, we never did though in the first twelve years when we were on at 12:30 AM we never did anything — a lot of mistakes were just left in. Much cheaper that way and the audience kind of loved it. They saw when things went wrong they loved it and of course Dave Letterman became a pro at just reacting to anything that went wrong, and of course you wanted to leave it in. Some of us missed those days, leaving it in, because they did edit a little more as they went along. But you know doing it five times a week, yeah, you do finally get used to it, finally.
I was going to ask if there was a “break glass in case of emergency” type protocol if you really had like a train wreck but it sounds like it just spontaneously fixed itself somehow.

I had some train wrecks on in the early days for sure that I couldn’t believe were on. They just went on, they just went by. Something crazy sticks in my mind though. Paul Simon making a rare TV appearance and he was going to sing with his acoustic guitar just on the panel with Dave, a beautiful song of his, “The Late, Great Johnny Ace” very nostalgic and wistful, kind of sad, sentimental. And it had a — it came to a point in the middle of it where it just got, you know, came to a slowed down pause as some of Paul Simon’s music does, and then would pick up again but before it could pick up again our assistant director the late, great Pete Fatovich who had to keep things moving, pressed that applause button and the audience applauded dutifully, and Paul wasn’t finished. Well we cut to commercial and I’m standing there saying, “Wait, wait, this is professional TV” but they just kept on, came back and Paul was just well I didn’t get to finish it but that’s the way it goes.

You know I was able to talk to Al Chez who was on the band for a while. And he said 90 percent of the time you got it. When you didn’t you learned the art of “I don’t know what I’m doing but it sounds like I do.”

Sure. I think he sums it up beautifully there. You have to, I mean it’s very exciting to live that way on a tightrope. And it’s the only way to fly on Dave Letterman’s show. He was truly as spontaneous as it looked. I don’t know if anybody else really is. The little experience that I’ve had going on some of the other guys’ shows, all of which I love for various reasons, but they do seem to rehearse these things. And then a guy drops in, you know, “Let’s take it from when he drops in spontaneous.” No Dave would never do that you know, just I don’t want to pretend, you know if it happens it’s happening. Let’s shoot what’s happening, no false pretext of a guy that’s pretending to drop in and whatever it
